# Idle gets stuck at 2000RPM

A friend of mine recently ran into a classic carburetor-era symptom: his 1989 Toyota Camry Wagon would occasionally lock its idle speed around 2000 RPM. The only way to reset the engine to a normal ~1000 RPM was to floor the accelerator, let the revs climb, and then release the pedal. That "kick" is the telltale sign of an air-fuel mixture that has stalled in a high-flow state until forced back down.

The instinctive response when facing idle instability is often to assume the throttle body butterfly valve is gummed up with carbon. In modern fuel-injected engines, a dirty throttle plate can indeed cause erratic idle behavior because the Electronic Control Unit (ECU) relies on precise airflow data. However, in older vehicles like this 1989 Camry, which likely uses a carburetor or a very early mechanical injection system, the physics are slightly different, and the diagnosis requires looking beyond just cleaning the butterfly.

The photos provided show a throttle body that appears mechanically sound but functionally insufficient after a thorough cleaning with Seafoam and a toothbrush. The key observation here is the nature of the "stuck" idle. When an engine idles at 2000 RPM, it is not merely running faster; it is likely experiencing a lean condition or a vacuum leak that prevents the ECU (or carburetor idle mixture screw) from dropping the speed to its target. If you clean the butterfly and the problem persists, the restriction isn't in the plate itself, but in the system's ability to regulate airflow at low speeds.

One common culprit for high-idle sticking is a vacuum leak upstream of the throttle body. On older engines, these leaks often originate from hardened rubber gaskets on the intake manifold or cracked vacuum hoses. If extra air enters the engine after the throttle plate, the ECU interprets this as a wide-open throttle condition or fails to adjust the idle mixture correctly, causing the RPM to spike. The "kick" maneuver works because it momentarily bypasses the leak by opening the throttle fully, allowing the fresh charge to overwhelm the unmetered air until the engine stabilizes at a higher baseline.

Another possibility is an issue with the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve or the idle mixture screw if the vehicle uses mechanical injection. Even though the butterfly was cleaned, the IAC might be clogged with debris that prevents it from opening just enough to maintain low-RPM stability. Cleaning the throttle body does not clean the IAC port behind the plenum. You would need to remove the IAC valve and inspect the pintle for carbon buildup or sticking.

Furthermore, check the EGR valve. If an Exhaust Gas Recirculation valve is stuck open, it introduces exhaust gases into the intake at idle, which can cause rough running or high-RPM locking in some configurations. While less common on a 1989 model depending on its specific drivetrain code, it is a standard failure mode for idle instability.

Before tearing down the intake manifold to hunt for vacuum leaks, use a carburetor cleaner spray around the base of all hose connections while the engine is idling. If the RPM fluctuates, you have found the leak. This is a non-invasive diagnostic step that often resolves high-idle issues without replacing major components.

If the vehicle is indeed fuel-injected and equipped with an IAC motor, consider cleaning the IAC port specifically. Sometimes the debris sits deep in the plenum behind the throttle body and never gets disturbed by spraying from the outside. A thorough inspection of the throttle position sensor (TPS) for proper voltage return at closed throttle is also critical; a TPS that doesn't register "closed" will command the engine to stay wide open, effectively locking the idle high.

In summary, cleaning the butterfly valve addresses airflow restriction but rarely solves the root cause of a high-speed lock-up unless that was the only issue. Focus your troubleshooting on vacuum integrity, IAC functionality, and sensor feedback loops. The solution likely lies in restoring the system's ability to meter air precisely at low loads rather than just clearing the main passage.
